body_markdown:
Yes, but this one has a little surprise.


If the state you live in doesn’t have annual motor vehicle inspections, fine. Go ahead and gloat. But if yours does, you’ve probably commiserated with the posts I’ve written over the years. On modern cars, you have check-engine light (CEL) and supplemental restraint system (SRS) indicators that can cause them to fail inspection. On vintage cars, you have myriad old wiring and bad ground issues that can trip you up by preventing something as trivial as a license plate light you never noticed from coming on. Of course, on both new and old, you have the ubiquitous horn and wiper test. My Z3 recently failed because the rubber on the wiper blades was shredded like wet spaghetti. (Hey, who uses their wipers on a convertible?)


But on the vintage cars, I’ve found that horns often inconveniently rear their non-functional heads at inspection time. The diaphragms in the actual horn elements in late 60s to early 1970s-era BMWs seem to develop the old-car equivalent of prostate and erectile issues and just kind of quit. You can sometimes adjust them back into usefulness with the screw on the back, but I often just buy whatever $10 substitute I can find.


I actually like horn-won’t-honk problems because they’re about the most easily solvable electrical troubleshooting issue you can have. Yeah, okay, maybe brake lights are easier, but then you have to bend down and check the switch on the pedal. With the horn, it’s all right in front of you.


I’ve gone through all this before, but let’s do it again. Your basic horn circuit has three major components: the horn itself, the horn contact, and the electrical relay that connects them. A relay is nothing more than a remote-controlled switch that allows a small amount of current to energize a little electromagnet that then pulls a set of contacts closed, allowing a much larger amount of current to flow without having to come through the passenger cabin.


The so-called DIN-standard relay numbering is that 30 and 87 are for the high-current side, and 86 and 85 are for the low-current side. Send 12 volts to 86 and ground 85 (or vice versa), and the electromagnet pulls a pair of electrical contacts together, connecting 30 to 87. If 30 is connected to battery voltage and 87 is connected to the thing you want to turn on, and if said thing is grounded, then said thing turns on—the horn honks, the lights blare, whatever it is. The only twist with the horn circuit is that on the low-current side, the horn button doesn’t send 12V to 86. Instead, the voltage is already there, and the horn button connects 85 to ground via the steering column.


The horn circuit on just about any older car. Note that the relay is switched on by the horn button completing the ground leg.


Rob Siegel


Because of this design, when a horn doesn’t honk, you can begin troubleshooting at one of three places—the horn itself, at the relay, or at the horn button. What I do is crack the key to accessories, lay my hand on the horn relay under the hood, then reach through the window to tap the horn button. If I feel the relay click, then the horn button and low-current side of the relay are working, and the problem is either in the high-current side of the relay or in the horn itself. But if the relay doesn’t click, the problem is either a blown fuse, the relay itself, the wiring, or the horn contact.


I’m writing about all this—again—because as the clock ran down on September, I was about to have a couple of cars with expired inspection stickers. The Z3, as I said, only needed wiper blades. But when I put my 1988 BMW E30 325is (a.k.a. “The FrankenThirty”) through its pre-inspection lights-wipers-horn paces, the horn was silent. I did the hand-on-the-relay test, and it didn’t click. I swapped relays, and that didn’t fix it. When I bought and resurrected the car a few years ago, I had problems with the ground leg of one of the adjacent relays, so I began focusing there.


There’s a trick you need to know to troubleshoot circuits with relays. The DIN-standard terminal numbers are almost always printed on the bottom of the relay, but not on the socket they’re plugged into. What you need to do is pull the relay out and hold it in your hand in the orientation that it goes in the socket.


Sorry the numbers are upside down, but they need to be consistent with the next photo.


Rob Siegel


Then, write those numbers on a small piece of paper, ***but transpose the numbers left-to-right, because the numbers in the socket are the mirror-image of the numbers on the bottom of the relay.*** Got it? Good.


The correctly labeled terminals in the relay socket.


Rob Siegel


With the socket terminals labeled, you can now test. Use a multimeter set to measure DC voltage, connect the black probe to ground, crack the key to accessories, and verify that there’s voltage at terminal 30. If so, take a jumper wire and run it from 30 to 87. This is commonly called “jumpering,” and it bypasses the relay (it’s doing what the electromagnet in the relay would do). It’s a lifesaver if, for example, your fuel pump relay or ECU relay fails. This is the horn relay, so other than for testing, I can’t imagine why you’d leave the jumper in. Unless you live in Manhattan or something.


Jumpering 30 to 87 to bypass the relay.


Rob Siegel


The jumper test made the horn blare, so I checked the low-current side of the circuit. 86 had voltage, but when I hit the horn button, 85 did not have continuity to ground.


Gotcha.


In multimeter-speak, “OL” means “over limit,” which for a resistance measurement means infinite resistance, which means terminal 85 was not connected to ground.


Rob Siegel


And so, with that, I turned my attention to the horn contact. On modern cars with buttons on the steering wheel for volume, radio station, and cruise control, electrical contact between the rotating steering wheel and the assembly behind it is achieved by a multi-contact device called a clock spring, but on a vintage car, there’s only the horn button, and it connects to a sprung “pin” that’s pressing against a circular ring. The ring may be on the back of the steering wheel and the contact on the column, or vice versa.


The horn contact on my BMW E9 3.0CSi with the stationary sprung contact and the steering-wheel-mounted contact ring.


Rob Siegel


I didn’t know which method the E30 used, but pulling the steering wheel off would tell me immediately.


I’m not sure I’ve ever had such a visceral “Well *there’s* your problem” reaction.


Well, okay then!


Rob Siegel


Obviously, the plastic neck in which the spring and the pin were housed had snapped clean off, leaving these parts dangling.


When I find something like this, I immediately sit down at the laptop, find the part number of the part I need, and get it on order. To my shock, this horn contact assembly, used in nearly every well-known BMW through the early 1990s except the venerable 2002 sedan, is no longer available.


What’s more, when I searched on eBay for a used one, I found that people wanted $70 for contacts with either broken or repaired plastic ears.


I went back into the garage and shifted into “What hack do I need to perform to get it through inspection?” mode. I found that heat-shrinking a piece of stiff tubing onto the stub of the snapped-off neck held the spring and pin well enough for the horn to make contact. I beat it to the inspection station, conscious that every turn of the wheel might cause the thing to fail.


It was inspection-worthy, but not much else.


Rob Siegel


Yeah, okay, I stopped at Trader Joe’s on the way home.


Rob Siegel


With the inspection issue behind me, I set about getting a permanent replacement part. I found many complaints about the part’s NLA status on users’ forums, and one enterprising fellow who sells a 3D-printed plastic housing that you can stuff your spring and pin into. But I contacted a guy I do business with in Connecticut who sells used E30 parts, and he said that he had a completely intact contact piece that he’d sell me for the cost of the damaged ones on eBay. The catch was that it was still riveted onto the steering lock piece because he didn’t want to risk damaging it by drilling out the rivets. These sort of “he’s near me, he’s helped me out” relationships are valuable, so rather than try to save $30 buying just the housing, I Venmo’d him the money, and the part arrived in a few days.


The steering lock assembly with the needed horn contact riveted on it.


Rob Siegel


Although the photo below shows a drill press in the background, I got the rivets out using a grinding bit on a Dremel tool, working from the back so I wouldn’t damage the plastic horn contact.


The valuable part freed.


Rob Siegel


I then needed to perform the analogous action on the car. This required removing a few pieces of trim to expose the bottom of the steering column. Here I used the Dremel on the front-facing side, as I didn’t care about damaging the plastic on the already-damaged horn contact.


You can see the Dremel marks where the rivets were.


Rob Siegel


And with that, the damaged piece came out, and the replacement was installed with M5 fasteners instead of rivets.


It sort of looks like a little anteater in there.


Rob Siegel


It’s funny. There are many times when I will go to ridiculous lengths to avoid spending $72 fixing a car, and would’ve spent hours cutting off the snapped-off neck of the horn contact and epoxying a cut-off housing of a ball-point pen, then crowing about what a great Hack Mechanic result it was. For some reason, I just wanted this fixed, and wanted to know that I wasn’t likely to have to deal with it again. Maybe the fact that it was something as trivial as a horn contact made me feel that it could have $72 of my money, but no more of my time. That’s a new dynamic for me. I need to think about what it means.


Geez, if this spreads from this simple example to, say, paying market value for cars in decent condition instead of spending months poring over Facebook Marketplace ads to find beat-up rides at bottom-feeder prices, we all could be in real trouble.


***
